content: An examination of the financial landscape reveals that obtaining definitive historical data regarding IT holding overhead ratios in South Africa for the period between 2020 and 2023 is highly constrained. As illustrated in the accompanying figure detailing Typical Overhead Ratios for South African IT Holding Companies (2020-2023), empirical benchmarks for the years 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 are currently unavailable, denoted by a complete absence of data points for each respective year. This data gap necessitates a broader reliance on macroeconomic indicators and future-oriented fiscal policies to infer the operational environments in which these IT holding companies navigated. For instance, recent analyses of South Africa's 2026 budget and fiscal consolidation plans project a national deficit of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product for March 2026, prioritizing macroeconomic stability over granular sector-level financial metrics [46] . Furthermore, governmental fiscal strategies highlight efforts to enhance fiscal credibility, with gross loan debt ratios expected to stabilize at 78.9 percent of gross domestic product [50] . Similarly, post-budget insights typically focus on macroeconomic factors such as fiscal stability and future economic growth trajectories, failing to offer the granular financial data required to establish historical overhead benchmarks for the IT sector [48] . The King IV framework underscored the importance of integrating financial, social, and environmental considerations into decision-making while promoting accountability and transparency within organizations, including holding entities in the IT sector .
